sentences.text: Archaeopteryx was similar in size to a Eurasian magpie.
This animal was roughly the size of a raven, featuring broad wings with rounded ends and a long tail relative to its body length.
Specimens are notable for well-developed, markedly asymmetrical flight feathers with vanes stabilized by a barb-barbule-barbicel arrangement similar to modern birds.
It possessed asymmetrical flight feathers and broad tail feathers similar to modern birds.
Archaeopteryx became a key piece of evidence supporting Darwin's theories on the origin of birds and evolution.

A 2011 study used scanning electron microscopy to analyze a single isolated feather, and comparisons with 87 modern bird species led researchers to calculate a 95% likelihood that the analyzed feather was originally black.
A 2002 scenario suggests Archaeopteryx used glides punctuated with shallow downstrokes to escape predators and cover distances.
A 2018 study reported Archaeopteryx had a flight stroke cycle closer to the grabbing motion of maniraptorans than modern birds.
The genus Archaeopteryx was named by Meyer in 1861.
Archaeopteryx was originally named based on a single feather found in 1861.
All known fossils of Archaeopteryx come from limestone deposits near Solnhofen, Germany.
The Unnumbered Specimen was originally classified as Compsognathus by the amateur collector Friedrich Müller.
The Mühlheim Specimen was initially considered a thirteenth Archaeopteryx but was reassigned to the distinct genus Alcmonavis upon its 2019 description.
Archaeopteryx is inferred to have had the ability to fly or glide.
Archaeopteryx most likely hunted small prey by seizing it with its jaws or claws.
The presence of advanced flight feathers in Archaeopteryx fossils suggests that feather evolution began before the Late Jurassic.
The Schamhaupten Specimen is the only known specimen lacking preserved feathers.

Most Archaeopteryx specimens likely drifted on their backs in the sea before becoming embedded in anoxic sediment, resulting in a characteristic death pose with the head, neck, and tail bent downward due to muscle relaxation and early decomposition.
A 2004 CT scan of the London specimen showed Archaeopteryx had a significantly larger brain than most dinosaurs, indicating it had the brain size necessary for flight.
A 2006 study found that Archaeopteryx's leg feathers formed up to 12% of its total airfoil.
Archaeopteryx lived during the Late Jurassic, between 150 and 148 million years ago.
John Ostrom considered Archaeopteryx to be remarkably similar to the theropod family Dromaeosauridae.
A 2009 histological study by Erickson, Norell, Zhongue, and others showed that Archaeopteryx had a relatively slow growth rate compared to modern birds.
All known skeletons of Archaeopteryx are believed to come from juvenile specimens.
Authors speculated that Archaeopteryx and the flightless kiwi had similar basal metabolic rates.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Archaeopteryx may have been a diurnal animal, similar to many modern birds.
In 1960, Swinton proposed placing Archaeopteryx lithographica on the official genera list, rendering alternative names like Griphosaurus and Griphornis invalid.
A 2007 review concluded that two distinct species, A. lithographica and A. siemensii, could be supported based on well-preserved specimens including the Thermopolis find.
In 2007, Phil Senter suggested that Jurapteryx, A. siemensii, and A. bavarica are junior synonyms of A. lithographica, arguing that their diagnostic features can be explained by ontogeny.
It is debated whether all discovered remains of Archaeopteryx belong to a single species or genus.
Archaeopteryx lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 150 million years ago.
The Schamhaupten Specimen is from the Painten Formation and is somewhat older than other Archaeopteryx specimens.
